details:
What it does and how it works

MARS-SOIL helps decide where, and how, to build on Mars when almost nothing has been measured directly. It uses two linked Excel workbooks. The first takes a Martian terrain described by 17 variables (topography, geology, grain size, cohesion, friction, ice and so on) and scores how closely it resembles five Earth analog sites, from 0 to 1. The second takes the soil and a proposed structure, then estimates bearing capacity with Terzaghi’s equation using Martian or lunar gravity. It also checks whether a pressurized habitat would be pushed upward out of the ground, and suggests a foundation type.

Benefits

  • Every number can be traced back to a visible formula, so the results can be audited.
  • Uncertainty is shown openly: conservative, central and optimistic scenarios, plus a count of how many variables were actually compared.
  • Teams can narrow down which regions deserve detailed study before spending on fieldwork.

Expected impact

The project is a preselection step, not a final design. Its value is in preventing bad early decisions, such as undersizing a foundation because Earth intuition was carried over to Mars. One result already shows this: with the example data, a pressurized module would generate roughly five times more uplift force than the combined weight holding it down, so a plain footing would fail without anchors or ballast.

Tools and technology

Both tools are Excel workbooks built with standard formulas and no macros. Python was used to check the Terzaghi calculations against published tables (under 3% difference). The inputs come from public sources such as NASA, JPL, USGS and USDA, plus Viking-era soil data. No special hardware was needed; an ordinary computer is enough. (This comes from the project documents; please add anything else your team actually used.)

What makes it creative

It treats missing data as part of the problem. Instead of waiting for Martian soil tests that may never come, it borrows knowledge from Earth analogs and turns vague statements like “this looks like Atacama” into a number. It also shows an effect many people don’t expect: lower gravity can make a cohesive soil safer to build on, while pressurization makes the structure much harder to hold down.

Factors the team considered

  • How reliable each data source is, and the difference between measured and estimated values.
  • Gravity’s two opposite effects: lighter structures, but lighter and less confining soil.
  • Pressurization uplift.
  • Realistic excavation limits for robots (2 m).
  • Known weaknesses, such as example inputs, expert-assigned scores and the exclusion of settlement and marsquakes, all listed in the documents.
